Electroplating materials selected for coating the sintered PA12 tensile specimens were sequentially layered equal parts of structural copper [Cu(s)], a ductile nickel bath (Traditional Nickle Sulfamate [TNS]), and hard nickel bath (Nickle deposit with a platinum anode [NDPA]).
Copper was deposited first as electroplating tests on SLS parts demonstrated its superior tolerance to the relatively rough powder surface.

Electroplating requires the cathode (the part being plated) to be conductive. This was accomplished by first preparing the surface to be electroless plated with a thin layer of autocatalytic Ni which was found to provide better bonding of the subsequent electroplating layers than covering the surface with a conductive paint.
Final conductive seed material is a 1-micron coating of electroless nickel applied in an electroless nickel bath.

The samples were extracted in two specific orientations: the transverse direction (TD) and the growth direction (GD). This allows characterization of how the material properties change with respect to orientation.

The printed batch included 144 ASTM-D638 tensile specimens [37] with 24 specimens in each orthotropic orientation (Fig. 2a). Each orientation included 12 standard specimens (3.2 mm thickness) and 12 thin specimens (0.8 mm thickness).

To achieve the desired scaled structural stiffness, the models must have relatively large overall dimensions with very thin thickness (0.8 mm) for the structural members (Fig. 1). Electroplating the model using the methods discussed in this paper results in increasing the model structural stiffness while maintaining the very thin thickness of structural members. Furthermore, electroplating the model creates a watertight layer to eliminate moisture absorption during testing in a towing tank.
Grains approximately 250 µm from the substrate have an average size of 74 nm, while grains 1.5 mm from the substrate are 120 nm in diameter.

Grain texture in the growth direction heavily favors the < 201 > directions, which also explains the change in properties of the growth direction as only 2 of the 12 FCC slips systems are active for the NDPA nickel.

The resultant strength of the material is much lower at the larger grain size. The cause of the increase in grain size is attributed to columnar grains forming within the deposit. These grains tend to grow in diameter as they progress.

The nickel deposited with a platinum anode (NDPA) bath, which falls within the Type 2 definition of the ASTM B689 standard, has a supplemental anode which is a titanium wire coated in a fine layer of platinum.
A Traditional Nickel Sulfamate (TNS) bath, which falls within the Type 1 definition of ASTM B689 standard, was also used.
The TNS sample appears to have minimal to no texture preference.
The NDPA nickel shows a strong < 201 > texture. The TNS sample shows no preferential texture.
It was found that the copper deposited FCC material had no directional dependence and behaved very isotropically, while the nickel deposited materials had variations in the two directions tested.

Overall, the average ϵf for the coated thin samples was 1.57%, which was only slightly less than the average ϵf of 1.70% for the coated standard samples.

The mechanical testing performed on the 18 coated standard samples and 18 coated thin samples followed the same procedures previously done by Slager et al. on uncoated samples [10] to allow a direct comparison between the coated and uncoated samples.
ANOVA analysis indicated that there was a statistically significant difference of EA based on orientation for all samples except the thin coated samples.
ANOVA analysis again indicated that there was a statistically significant difference of σy based on orientation for all samples except the thin coated samples.
ANOVA analysis again indicated that there was a statistically significant difference of UTS based on orientation for all samples except the thin coated samples.

While the ANOVA and t test analysis did not definitively identify the impact of orientation of print orientation on coated samples with the samples used, the incorporation of DOA analysis more clearly highlighted these impacts. Future research with an increased sample size (larger than the three used for this study) could provide further insight into whether a difference more definitely exists.

The sectioning done at room temperature did not indicate any separation at the PA12/coating interface; however, plastic deformation (“smearing”) of the PA12 made it difficult to identify the interface. Sectioning at cryogenic temperatures (Fig. 13b-c) mitigated most of the plastic deformation during sectioning but did appear to cause some damage that may have pulled the PA12 away from the coating.
In all cases, it does appear the coating filled in most of the rough particulate SLS surface and bonded to the PA12 core.

Though the overall fracture mode appears to be relatively brittle for both the sintered PA12 and the metal coating, when compared to the sectioned samples (Fig. 13), it does appear the sintered PA12 core elastically deformed more than the metal coating which caused debonding at the PA12/metal interface.
Overall, fractography and sectioning indicated the separation between the PA12 and metal coating occurred during plastic deformation.

Electroplating also opens the door to customizing part properties by calculating required coating thickness using ROM, which was demonstrated for EA with an average deviation from ROM predicted values to measured values of 5.2% for standard samples and 7.5% for thin samples. ROM was not as accurate of a material property prediction tool for properties further in the plastic region, such as σy, UTS, and εf, suggesting that further research is prudent to expand this predictive capability beyond EA.
